239.title: The five thieves
239.hook: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride rob the house of the mind
239.howItsDone: Sikhs are commonly taught the five thieves, kaam, krodh, lobh, moh and ahankaar, as the main obstacles inside a person, to be overcome through remembering the Name, honest living and the company of the sangat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nadar, the kindly glance. Your line was the glance comes. Did you give someone a look that said I see you? Today, a darker picture, and a very practical one. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

You wake up, walk into the kitchen, and something is off. A drawer is open. Your bag is on the wrong chair. Your wallet is gone. Nobody smashed a window. The back door was simply unlocked, and someone quiet came in while you slept. The worst part isn't the money. It's realizing they were in your house and you didn't notice. Good thieves don't announce themselves. They slip in when you're tired, distracted or not paying attention, and they take what matters most. The Granth uses exactly this picture, and it says there isn't one thief but five, and they aren't outside. They live in the house.
screen: `A DRAWER LEFT OPEN.` → `THE BACK DOOR WAS UNLOCKED.` → `FIVE THIEVES, INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is panj chor. Panj is five, the same panj that's in the name Punjab, the land of five rivers. Chor is a thief, a word still used across North India. The five thieves. The Granth names them again and again. Kaam: lust, desire that grabs. Krodh: anger. Lobh: greed, always wanting more. Moh: attachment, clinging to people and things as if they could never change. And ahankaar: pride, the swollen I. One hymn in Sorath puts it plainly: inside this body live five thieves, lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, and they steal the nectar, while the self-willed person doesn't even notice. The house is the body and the mind. The treasure is the nectar, the Name, the peace we talked about yesterday and the day before. And the thieves don't break in. They already live there. Notice what that means. The Granth doesn't mainly point at bad people out there. It points inward, at the five movements every human being knows. Some Sikh teachers add something fair: each of the five begins as a natural energy. Desire, anger at injustice, wanting enough, loving people, a healthy sense of self. They become thieves when they take over the house and run it. So the first step isn't to fight them blindly. It's to know them: their faces, their habits, which door they use. A thief you've recognized is already half caught. Tomorrow, who guards the house.
screen: `PANJ CHOR — FIVE THIEVES.` · `LUST, ANGER, GREED, ATTACHMENT, PRIDE.` · `THEY LIVE INSIDE THE HOUSE.` · `KNOW THEIR FACES.` · then, large: `KNOW THE THIEVES.`

segments.voice: Sit quietly and walk through your day so far, like checking the rooms of a house. Which of the five has been most active? Anger, flaring at someone? Greed, wanting more? Attachment, gripping? Pride, needing to be right? Desire, pulling at you? Don't judge it. Just name it, softly, the way you'd name a visitor: ah, it's you. Then let the naming be enough, and rest in your breath, the house quieter now. The bell holds the time.
Panj chor. The five thieves: lust, anger, greed, attachment and pride, living in the house of the mind and stealing its treasure.
Your line: know the thieves. Today, when one of the five shows up, name it quietly in your head, and watch how much of its power goes. Day two hundred thirty-nine.

240.title: The five virtues
240.hook: truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love guard the same house
240.howItsDone: Sikhs are commonly taught the five virtues, sat, santokh, daya, nimrata and pyaar, alongside the five thieves, and many teachers pair each virtue with the thief it answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, panj chor, the five thieves. Your line was know the thieves. Did you catch one and name it? Today, who stands guard in the same house. Day two hundred forty.

Yesterday's house had an unlocked back door and five thieves already inside. So what do you do? You could buy a bigger lock. You could sit up all night with a flashlight, glaring at every shadow. People try that with their own minds: white-knuckle willpower, fighting every bad impulse head-on. It's exhausting, and it rarely lasts. Now think of a house that feels safe. Usually it isn't safe because of locks. It's safe because of who lives there: people who are kind, honest, settled, glad to be home. Thieves don't like a full, lit, busy house. The Granth's answer to the five thieves is five guards.
screen: `A BIGGER LOCK?` → `A FLASHLIGHT ALL NIGHT?` → `A FULL, LIT HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Sikh teaching names five virtues. Sat: truth, being true all the way through. Santokh: contentment, the enough you met in Pauri 10. Daya: compassion. Nimrata: humility. And pyaar: love. A quick, honest note. You won't find these five printed as a numbered list on one page of the Granth. The list is a way Sikh teachers gather what the Granth says across hundreds of hymns, and each of the five is everywhere in it. You've already heard them in the Japji. Pauri 16: dhaul dharam daiaa kaa poot. The bull that holds up the earth is dharma, the child of compassion, and contentment is in the next line too, though commentators read its exact role there in more than one way. Pauri 18, Guru Nanak calling himself lowly: humility. Pauri 21: listening, trusting, and love in the mind. And sach, truth, from the Mool Mantar on. Now the part that makes the picture work. Many Sikh teachers pair each guard with a thief. Humility stands against pride. Compassion against anger. Contentment against greed. Love, wide and giving, against attachment that clings. And truth against lust, desire that grabs what isn't true to the moment. The guards don't beat the thieves in a fistfight. They fill the house. When humility is home, pride has no room to sit down. So instead of staring at the shadows all night, you practice one guard, today, and the house slowly changes who lives in it.
screen: `SAT, SANTOKH, DAYA, NIMRATA, PYAAR.` · `GATHERED FROM ACROSS THE GRANTH.` · `EACH GUARD FACES A THIEF.` · `FILL THE HOUSE.` · then, large: `FIVE GUARDS AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Think of yesterday's thief, the one most active in you. Now find its guard. If it was anger, compassion. If greed, contentment. If pride, humility. If clinging, a wider love. If grabbing, truth. Picture that guard standing at your door, calm and awake. Breathe in, and let that quality fill your chest. Breathe out, and let it fill the room. Keep breathing it in and out, a house filling with light. The bell holds the time.
Nimrata, humility. Truth, contentment, compassion, nimrata and love: gathered from across the Granth, five guards for the same house the thieves live in.
Your line: five guards at the door. Today, choose one of the five and practice it on purpose, once, in a real moment. Day two hundred forty.

241.title: Maya, the passing pull
241.hook: the pull of the passing world, attractive and fleeting, is called maya
241.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of maya as the pull of wealth, status and attachment; the Gurus taught living as householders in the world, working and raising families, while remembering the Name so as not to be ruled by that pull.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five virtues: truth, contentment, compassion, humility and love. Your line was five guards at the door. Which guard stood up for you? Today, the pull those guards are guarding against. Day two hundred forty-one.

You open your phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later you're watching a stranger restore a rusty knife, and you've added a jacket to a cart. Nothing bad happened. Everything was pretty. The knife was shiny, the jacket was soft, the video was calming. And none of it is what you meant to do with those forty minutes. It's a familiar pull: bright, sweet, and gone the moment you look away. The Gurus had a word for it, long before phones. Today it's maya.
screen: `CHECK THE WEATHER.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `ALL OF IT PRETTY.` → `MAYA.`

segments.voice: Maya is an old Indian word, and different traditions use it differently. In some Hindu schools it can mean the world as a kind of illusion. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the stress falls somewhere else. In the Granth's telling, the world is real; the Creator made it and lives in it. Maya is the pull of the passing parts of it: money, status, comfort, attachment, anything bright that promises to last and doesn't. The problem isn't that things are fake. It's that we lean our whole weight on things that were only ever passing through. The Granth gives maya many pictures. Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, has a short salok near the very end of the book. As a bubble rises on water and vanishes, he says, so the world is made; Nanak says, listen, friend. The bubble is real. It even has a rainbow on it. It just isn't a place to live. Another hymn calls maya a snake that has wrapped itself around the world. And notice what Sikh teaching does not say. It doesn't say run to the forest, give up your job, leave your family. The Gurus taught a householder's path: work, family, and the Name. The ideal is to live in the middle of the bright, busy world and not be owned by it, like a lotus that grows in water and stays dry. That's the question maya asks on an ordinary afternoon: am I using this, or is it using me? Pretty isn't the enemy. Forgetting that it's passing is.
screen: `AN OLD WORD, USED MANY WAYS.` · `NOT FAKE — JUST PASSING.` · `A BUBBLE ON WATER.` · `IN THE WORLD, NOT OWNED BY IT.` · then, large: `PRETTY, AND PASSING.`

segments.voice: Think of one pull that got you today: a screen, a purchase, a worry about how you look, a craving. Don't scold yourself for it. Just picture it clearly, the way it shines. Now picture it as a bubble on water, catching the light. Say to yourself, quietly: pretty, and passing. Then let your attention come back to the breath, which is also passing, and also here. Stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Maya. In the Guru Granth Sahib, the pull of the passing world: bright, attractive, and gone. Not a lie, just not a home.
Your line: pretty, and passing. Today, when something pulls at you, pause for one breath before you follow it, and name it: pretty, and passing. Day two hundred forty-one.

242.title: Gurmukh and manmukh
242.hook: the one facing the Guru and the one facing only their own mind
242.howItsDone: Sikhs use gurmukh for a person oriented toward the Guru's teaching and manmukh for one led by their own mind; many turn to the Guru Granth Sahib, through daily reading or kirtan, as the way of facing the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya, the passing pull. Your line was pretty, and passing. Did you catch one bright thing tugging at you, and pause? Today, which way you're facing when it tugs. Day two hundred forty-two.

Young sunflowers do something lovely. In the morning their heads turn east, toward the light, and by evening they've followed it west. Now suppose one sunflower that decided to face a mirror instead. It would see a very handsome sunflower. It would also, slowly, stop growing. Where you face shapes what you become. The Guru Granth Sahib has two words for the two ways a person can face, and they appear again and again, on page after page. Today's word is the first of them: gurmukh.
screen: `A FIELD FACING EAST.` → `ONE FACING A MIRROR.` → `WHERE YOU FACE, YOU GROW.`

segments.voice: Gurmukh is two words joined. Gur, the Guru. Mukh, the face, or the mouth. So a gurmukh is someone whose face is turned toward the Guru. Its opposite is manmukh. Man is the mind, the restless self; a manmukh faces only their own mind, their own wants, their own reflection. Sikh teachers often read these less as two tribes of people, good ones and bad ones, than as two directions, and a person can turn either way in the course of a single afternoon. The hymns paint them clearly. The manmukh, they say, is busy and anxious, driven by the five thieves we met a few days ago, always chasing the next thing, like someone wandering in the dark. The gurmukh is not someone with a special title. It's someone who listens to the Guru's word, remembers the Name, works honestly, and serves, and so finds a kind of steadiness. Guru Nanak's great conversation with the yogis, the Sidh Gosht, keeps coming back to this word: it is through the Guru, facing the Guru, that one comes to understand. And remember: for Sikhs, the Guru is now the Guru Granth Sahib, the Word itself. So facing the Guru can be as simple as opening the book, listening to a hymn, or letting a line of it question you before you act. The practical test is small. Before I do this, which way am I facing? Toward what I'd do if I were listening to the Guru, or toward the mirror?
screen: `GUR + MUKH — FACING THE GURU.` · `MAN + MUKH — FACING YOUR OWN MIND.` · `TWO DIRECTIONS, NOT TWO TRIBES.` · `THE GURU IS NOW THE WORD.` · then, large: `FACE THE GURU.`

segments.voice: Think of one choice waiting for you today: a message to answer, a task, a conversation. Picture yourself turned toward the mirror, choosing only for your own comfort. Now picture turning, the way a sunflower turns, toward the best you know: truth, kindness, the Guru's word if that's your path. Notice how the choice looks from there. Settle on one good turn you'll make. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Gurmukh. The one whose face is turned toward the Guru. Its opposite, manmukh, faces only its own mind. Anyone can turn either way.
Your line: face the guru. Today, before one choice, ask which way you're facing, and turn toward good once. Day two hundred forty-two.

243.title: Sahaj: effortless ease
243.hook: a natural, balanced calm that comes when striving settles
243.howItsDone: Sahaj is a key word in Sikh scripture for natural, balanced poise; the Anand Sahib, which uses it in its first verse, is sung at many Sikh ceremonies and a short form is recited at the close of congregational services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurmukh, the one whose face is turned toward the Guru. Your line was face the guru. Did you make one good turn? Today, what that turning feels like from the inside. Day two hundred forty-three.

Try to fall asleep. Really try. Squeeze your eyes, count harder, will yourself unconscious. It doesn't work, does it? Or think of a glass of muddy water. Stir it to clear it and it only gets cloudier. Set it on the table and leave it, and slowly the mud sinks and the water goes clear. Some good things can't be grabbed. They come when the grabbing stops. The Gurus had a word for the calm that arrives that way. Today it's sahaj.
screen: `TRY HARDER TO SLEEP.` → `STIR THE MUDDY WATER.` → `LEAVE IT, AND IT CLEARS.`

segments.voice: Sahaj means natural, easy, what comes of itself. The word is old: yogis and poets in India used it for a state beyond effort. In the Guru Granth Sahib it becomes one of the great words for a settled, balanced life. You hear it in phrases like sahaj subhai, naturally, of its own accord, and sahaj samadhi, a stillness that isn't a trance in a cave but calm in the middle of ordinary days. Here's the heart of it. Sahaj isn't laziness, and it isn't giving up. The Sikh way has plenty of effort in it: rising early, work, service, prayer. Sahaj is what happens to all that effort when the ego stops gripping it. Haumai, the self-centered I we met last week, is always straining: to be noticed, to win, to control. When it quiets, the same work goes on, but lighter. The Anand Sahib, the song of bliss by Guru Amar Das, opens with anand, bliss, and sahaj arrives in the very next line. Its first verse, in paraphrase: O my mother, bliss has come, for I have found the True Guru, and I found him with ease, sahaj. Not by conquering, not by some heroic feat. With ease. The hymns often picture sahaj as a home, the place the restless mind finally comes back to and sits down. So on an ordinary Tuesday, sahaj might look like this: doing the dishes without fighting them. Listening without planning your reply. Working hard, and not being eaten by it. The water clears when you stop stirring.
screen: `SAHAJ — NATURAL, OF ITSELF.` · `NOT LAZY — EFFORT WITHOUT GRIP.` · `ANAND SAHIB: FOUND WITH EASE.` · `A HOME THE MIND COMES BACK TO.` · then, large: `EASE.`

segments.voice: Choose one small thing you can do right now: a sip of water, a stretch, folding your hands. Do it slowly, as if nothing is waiting. No hurry, no performance. Notice the moment the effort stops pushing and just moves. Then let the breath breathe itself. Don't manage it; let it come and go, the way muddy water settles on its own. The bell holds the time.
Sahaj. Natural, balanced ease; the calm that comes when striving settles, and the ego stops gripping the work.
Your line: ease. Today, do one ordinary thing slowly and easily, without fighting it, and notice what changes. Day two hundred forty-three.

244.title: The soul as a bride
244.hook: many hymns speak as a bride longing for her Husband Lord, a picture of the soul's love
244.howItsDone: At a Sikh wedding, the Anand Karaj, the four verses of the Laavan by Guru Ram Das are read and sung as the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib, and they're understood as describing both the marriage and the soul's union with God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sahaj, the ease that comes when the grip lets go. Your line was ease. Did one ordinary thing go slowly and easily? Today, the Granth's warmest picture of the soul. Day two hundred forty-four.

The Gurus were all men. And yet, again and again in the Guru Granth Sahib, they sing in a woman's voice. A young bride, waiting at the window. Getting ready, wondering if her beloved will come. Asking her friends how they won his love. Guru Nanak does it. Guru Arjan does it. Bhagat Kabir, whose hymns sit beside theirs, does it too. Why would they choose that voice, of all voices, to speak about God? Today's word opens it: suhagan.
screen: `THE GURUS WERE MEN.` → `THEY SING AS A BRIDE.` → `WHY THAT VOICE?`

segments.voice: Suhagan means the happily married bride, the one united with her husband. Its opposite in the hymns is duhagan, the bride left alone, forgotten. In this picture, God is the Husband, the Beloved, and every soul is the bride, whether the person singing is a man or a woman. It's not a statement about men and women. It's a picture of love. In the hymns' picture, the bride can't win love by arguing or bargaining. She can get ready, keep faith, and wait. So the hymns ask: how does a bride become suhagan? Not through jewelry, not through fancy clothes, they say, but through humility, sweet speech, and love. In one of Guru Nanak's hymns in Tilang, the bride is told to go and ask the happy wives how they won the Husband, and the answer is, roughly: accept whatever he does as good, drop your own cleverness and your own commands, and do as he says. That's hukam, the order, turned into romance. The picture comes closest to home at a Sikh wedding. The Laavan, four verses by Guru Ram Das, are sung while the couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib. They're a wedding song, and they're also about the soul's marriage to God, stage by stage. So every Sikh wedding is two weddings at once. And the picture says something tender: in these hymns, what lies between a person and God isn't fear or duty. It's longing, and belonging.
screen: `SUHAGAN — THE UNITED BRIDE.` · `EVERY SOUL IS THE BRIDE.` · `NOT JEWELS — HUMILITY AND LOVE.` · `THE LAAVAN: TWO WEDDINGS AT ONCE.` · then, large: `THE SOUL IS A BRIDE.`

segments.voice: Take a pen, or the notes on your phone. Write one line of longing. It can be for God, if that's your language, or for peace, for someone you miss, for the person you hope to become. Just one honest line, in your own words: I wish, I miss, I'm waiting for. Read it once, quietly. Then set it down and sit with the feeling it leaves, without fixing it. The bell holds the time.
Suhagan. The bride united with her beloved. In the Granth, a picture of the soul, any soul, joined with God through love and humility.
Your line: the soul is a bride. Today, keep the line of longing you wrote somewhere you'll see it again tonight. Day two hundred forty-four.

245.title: Birha: longing
245.hook: the ache of separation is honored in the Granth as part of love
245.howItsDone: Hymns of longing, including the Barah Maha of the twelve months, are sung in Sikh kirtan; many gurdwaras recite the Barah Maha in Majh on sangrand, the first day of each month in the Punjabi calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suhagan, the bride united with her beloved. Your line was the soul is a bride. Did you read your line of longing again last night? Today, the longing itself, and the end of a week. Day two hundred forty-five.

Think of an airport arrivals hall. People holding signs, holding flowers, craning their necks at the sliding doors. Some have waited months. Nobody would say those people love less because they're waiting. If anything, the waiting is the love, made visible. Most of us treat missing someone, or missing God, as a problem to fix fast. The Guru Granth Sahib does something unexpected with that ache. It doesn't hide it. It honors it, and gives it a name. Today's word: birha.

Birha is the pain of separation: the bride from the beloved, the soul from God. Yesterday's bride was united. Today's bride is at the window, still waiting. And the Granth gives her a lot of room. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha walks through the twelve months of the year, and in month after month the bride aches for her beloved, in the heat, in the rains, in the cold. Guru Nanak has his own Barah Maha too. The longing isn't treated as failure. It's treated as a sign that love is alive. The boldest line comes from Sheikh Farid, a Sufi poet of the Punjab whose couplets the Gurus kept in the Granth; we'll meet him properly in two weeks. He says, in the original: birhaa birhaa aakheeai birhaa too sultaan. People keep saying separation, separation; separation, you are the king. And then: the body in which this longing never rises, know it as a cremation ground. Strong words. The ache, Farid says, is proof of life. A heart that never misses anything isn't peaceful. It's asleep. Why would a tradition honor pain? Because longing points. You can only miss what you love. So in the Granth, birha is not the opposite of love. It's love, facing the door. That's the week's thread, too. This week: the five thieves and nimrata, maya's passing pull, facing the Guru, the ease of sahaj, the soul as a bride, and now birha. Every one of them is about where the heart is facing.
screen: `BIRHA — THE ACHE OF SEPARATION.` · `TWELVE MONTHS OF WAITING.` · `FARID: SEPARATION, YOU ARE KING.` · `YOU ONLY MISS WHAT YOU LOVE.` · then, large: `LONGING IS LOVE TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one longing you carry: a person far away, someone who has died, a hope that hasn't come, or, if you pray, a longing for God. Don't try to fix it or push it away. Sit beside it, kindly, the way you'd sit beside a friend in an arrivals hall. Let it be what it is: a sign of love. Breathe with it. The bell holds the time.
Birha. The ache of separation, honored in the Granth as part of love. This week's words: the five thieves, nimrata, maya, gurmukh, sahaj, suhagan, birha.
Your line: longing is love too. Today, when you miss someone or something, don't rush past it; let it remind you what you love. Day two hundred forty-five.

fork.setup: you're aching for someone you can't reach. what does the Granth's picture of birha suggest?
options: pretend you feel nothing.
treat the ache as a sign of love, and sit with it kindly.
decide love must have ended.
fork.reveal: Farid calls separation the king: a heart that never longs is asleep. you only miss what you love.

original.note: Gurmukhi: birha, the pain of separation; Farid's salok calls it sultaan, the king.

trapdoor: what you thought: longing means something is wrong.
what it means: in the Granth, the ache of separation is part of love, and a heart that never longs is asleep.
what a scholar hears: birha is a central mood of Punjabi and Sufi poetry; Farid's salok (Ang 1379) crowns it sultaan, and the Barah Maha genre maps it onto the twelve months.
